changes.summary: Visual culture from the Indigenous peoples of the Americas is on view in an open gallery space along the east corridor of the main building. Featuring a rotating selection from the more than 800 works in the museum’s holdings, the principal display includes historically important examples from Mesoamerica, the Pacific Northwest, and the Arctic. Works from the Indigenous Americas are also on view in A Surrealist Wunderkammer. John and Dominique de Menil lived in South America from 1941 to 1944, primarily residing in Caracas, Venezuela, with some longer stays in Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina. Before returning to Houston, the couple collected ceramic figurines and fragments dating to the ancient civilizations of West Mexico and South America. By the 1950s, they had assembled a small collection of about 40 examples. Stirred by their philanthropic initiatives and exhibition projects at the University of St. Thomas and Rice University, their collection rapidly grew over the next two decades to include works from most artistic traditions in the Indigenous Americas. The museum works collaboratively with communities of Indigenous peoples whose cultural heritage is held by the museum. Many works from the Indigenous Americas are on long-term loan to the Menil from the Rock Foundation, which Adelaide de Menil and anthropologist Edmund Carpenter (1922–2011) founded in 1976. The couple were instrumental in the acquisition of objects from the Pacific Northwest and Arctic. Potlatch masks and headgear, textile garments, finely carved wooden chests, spoons, and other implements from the Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, Nuu-chah-nulth, and other Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest are well represented. Carpenter, art historian Bill Holm (1925–2020), and Haida artist Bill Reid (1920–1998) contributed to the interpretation of this collection during the 1970s.
